analysis.one_liner: Requires voting machines to print a paper record voters can check to confirm their vote.
analysis.headline: A bill requiring paper records of every electronic vote drew 38 House cosponsors, but was never acted on after referral to committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Help America Vote Act of 2002 to require every federal voting system to give voters a paper record showing how their vote will be recorded. Voters would check the paper record to make sure it matches their intent, and could correct any error before the vote becomes final. The paper record would be kept as the permanent record of each vote, and federal voting guidelines would have to include standards for the security of electronic voting data [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in federal elections, who would get a way to confirm on paper that the machine recorded their vote as intended, giving elections a physical record that can be audited or recounted if electronic results are in doubt.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All voters casting ballots on machines

how_it_helps.text: After a voter enters a vote, the machine must print an auditable paper record showing how the vote will be recorded, and the voter must use it to verify the vote shown is the vote intended [S2] [S3].
If the paper record does not match the voter's intent, the voter can change the ballot and correct the error, and the system must produce a new paper record reflecting the correction [S2] [S3].

Once verified, the paper record becomes the permanent record of the vote and may not be removed from the polling place except by election officials for recounts or other official purposes under state law [S2] [S3].
Voluntary voting system guidelines would have to include measures to ensure the security of any data transmitted or received electronically by voting systems [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Electronic voting machine makers, who would have to add printers or retrofit existing paperless touchscreen machines to produce paper records, and state and local election offices that would bear the cost of those upgrades before federal elections.
analysis.who_pays_short: Voting machine vendors and election offices

drawbacks.text: The requirement would have taken effect as if part of the 2002 law, giving election offices and machine makers little lead time to retrofit or replace paperless machines before elections, a cost and logistics burden the bill text does not address with funding [S3].

The bill stops at requiring a paper record for the voter to see; it does not itself mandate routine audits or recounts using those records, so the guarantee of an accurate count depends on state laws already allowing recounts or official use of the records [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: with more Americans voting on paperless touchscreen machines in the 2004 elections, a verified paper record is the basic safeguard that lets a close result be checked and a machine error or data loss be detected. The cost is a retrofit for machine vendors and election offices, which is the unavoidable price of a paper trail, though the bill's own structure — retroactive effective date, no dedicated funding, no mandated use of the records in audits — would have made it harder to carry out than its goal suggests.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Representative Steve King of Iowa introduced the bill on April 21, 2004, with 38 Republican cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on House Administration [S1] [S3] [S4] [S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill — no markup and no vote — and the Congress ended January 3, 2005, without the bill ever reaching the House floor [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Paperless voting machine vendors, who faced no federal requirement to retrofit their touchscreen machines with printers, and election officials who did not have to fund a paper-trail upgrade on the bill's timeline.

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 21, 2004, to require voting systems to produce a voter-verifiable paper record of each vote [S1] [S5].

against.name: Rep. Bob Ney
against.role: Chair, House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it sat without action until the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 38 cosponsors were Republicans and there was never a vote, so no one had to take a recorded position on it [S4] [S5].

industries.note: In 2004, many jurisdictions were buying paperless touchscreen machines from vendors such as Diebold, ES&S, and Sequoia, and the bill would have forced printers or retrofit costs onto machines that worked fine for the vendors without a paper trail. Its requirements directly cut against the companies' existing product lines and contracts, while a verifiable paper record is the safeguard voters would use to catch machine errors.
